issues.legal_issue: A state empowered to regulate the supply and purchase of sugarcane may fix a price higher than the central minimum price.
material_facts: The central government had fixed a minimum price for sugarcane.
The state had enacted a law regulating the supply and purchase of sugarcane, including in areas reserved or assigned to sugar factories.
Growers in reserved or assigned areas were subject to restrictions on whom they could supply and when they could supply sugarcane.
The state fixed an advised price above the central minimum price.
issues.conclusion: The state had power under its sugarcane regulation law to fix a higher price, and that price could be enforced against sugar factories.
issues.legal_principle: The central price was a minimum, not an exhaustive price determination, and the state law's power to regulate sugarcane supply and purchase included the incidental power to determine price. The Court relied on Sections 15 and 16 of the U.P. Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1953, the related Rules and 1954 Order, and the broad meaning of “regulate” in State of Tamil Nadu v. Hindu Stone, K. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu, VSR & Oil Mills v. State of A.P., Jiyajeerao Cotton Mills v. M.P. Electricity Board, and Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar. It also relied on Maharashtra Rajya Sahkari Sakkar Karkhana Sangh v. State of Maharashtra, State of M.P. v. Jaora Sugar Mills, and SKG Sugar v. State of Bihar. Tika Ramji was distinguished because it arose under the earlier central order and before the state had fixed a price under its regulatory power; Kothari Sugars was distinguished because the state there lacked a statutory basis for its price announcement.

predicates.challenge_to_state_cane_price: A party to a dispute over the price of sugarcane challenges a state-fixed price.
predicates.state_law_regulates_cane_supply_and_purc: A state law authorizes regulation of the supply or purchase of sugarcane.
predicates.state_price_exceeds_central_minimum: The state-fixed sugarcane price is higher than the minimum price fixed by the central authority.
predicates.state_may_fix_and_enforce_higher_cane_pr: The state may fix and enforce a sugarcane price higher than the central minimum.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a state-fixed cane price arises under a state law regulating cane supply or purchase, and the state price exceeds the central minimum, the state may fix and enforce the higher price.

issues.legal_issue: A state price above the central minimum price is not repugnant to the central price requirement when the central requirement establishes only a minimum.
material_facts: The central order prohibited sale or purchase of sugarcane below the central minimum price.
The state price at issue was higher than the central minimum price.
The state and central price requirements could both be complied with by paying the higher state price.
issues.conclusion: There was no repugnancy between the central minimum price and the higher state price.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254(1) of the Constitution, repugnancy requires inconsistent provisions operating in the same field such that both cannot operate or be obeyed. A higher state price does not conflict with a central minimum because payment of the higher price satisfies the minimum requirement. The Court relied on Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh, M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India, Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State of Bihar, National Engineering Industries v. Sri Kishan Bhageria, and S. Satyapal Reddy v. Government of A.P.

predicates.challenge_to_state_cane_price: A party to a dispute over the price of sugarcane challenges a state-fixed price.
predicates.central_price_is_only_a_minimum: The central price requirement sets a floor and does not prohibit a higher price.
predicates.state_price_is_higher_than_central_minim: The state-fixed sugarcane price is higher than the central minimum price.
predicates.no_repugnancy_between_the_price_requirem: The state and central price requirements are not repugnant and may operate together.

issues.definition: Where a challenge concerns a state price above a central price that operates only as a minimum, the two price requirements can operate together without repugnancy.

issues.legal_issue: A sugar factory cannot avoid a price term in a regulated sugarcane supply agreement merely because the agreement was required by law or the factory did not voluntarily accept that term.
material_facts: The state regulatory scheme required growers or their cooperative societies and sugar factories to enter into prescribed supply agreements.
The scheme restricted growers’ ability to supply cane elsewhere and imposed consequences for failure to supply the required quantity.
The agreements assured factories a continuous supply of sugarcane from reserved or assigned areas.
The state-fixed price was included in the supply agreements or related purchase records.
The factories sought to rely on lack of voluntary consent to avoid the price term.
issues.conclusion: The price term in the regulated supply agreements was binding; statutory compulsion did not make the agreements invalid or the price unenforceable.
issues.legal_principle: Price is an essential element of a sale, but a sale or contract does not cease to be valid merely because law regulates or compels its formation. The Court relied on Sections 4 and 5 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, and Sections 2, 10, and 13–15 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as discussed in Andhra Sugars v. State of Andhra Pradesh. It also relied on Indian Steel & Wire Products v. State of Madras, Salar Jung Sugar Mills v. State of Mysore, Sukhnandan Saran Dinesh Kumar v. Union of India, State of M.P. v. Jaora Sugar Mills, and SKG Sugar v. State of Bihar. The factories could not accept the benefits of the regulated supply arrangement while rejecting its price term.

rule.if: dispute_over_regulated_cane_supply_agreement and agreement_requires_cane_supply and factory_receives_assured_supply_benefit and state_price_is_in_agreement

predicates.dispute_over_regulated_cane_supply_agree: A dispute concerns the enforceability of a sugarcane supply agreement made under a regulatory scheme.
predicates.agreement_requires_cane_supply: The agreement or governing scheme requires the grower or cooperative society to supply sugarcane to the factory.
predicates.factory_receives_assured_supply_benefit: The factory receives the benefit of an assured supply of sugarcane under the regulated arrangement.
predicates.state_price_is_in_agreement: The state-fixed price is included as a term of the supply agreement or its related purchase records.
predicates.agreement_price_is_binding_despite_statu: The price term remains binding even though the agreement was required by the regulatory scheme.

issues.definition: When a regulated cane supply agreement requires supply, benefits the factory with assured cane, and includes the state-fixed price, that price term binds the factory despite statutory compulsion.

issues.legal_issue: A state without a law regulating sugarcane supply and purchase cannot unilaterally fix a sugarcane price, although the parties may agree to a price above the central minimum.
material_facts: No state enactment regulated the supply and purchase of sugarcane in the relevant state.
The state acknowledged that it was not fixing the advised price under statutory authority and said it would consult growers and mills before recommending an agreed price.
The central order fixed a minimum price and did not prohibit parties from agreeing to pay more.
issues.conclusion: The state lacked power to fix the price unilaterally, but sugar mills and growers remained free to agree on a price above the central minimum.
issues.legal_principle: The state's regulatory power to fix a higher price depends on statutory authority; absent such authority, a unilateral state price announcement has no statutory basis. The central Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966 establishes a minimum price, leaving parties free to agree on a higher price. The Court distinguished State of Tamil Nadu v. Kothari Sugars and Chemicals because it concerned a payment made without contractual or statutory basis, rather than a higher price established by a valid state regulatory law or an agreement.

predicates.challenge_to_state_price_announcement: A party challenges a state announcement fixing the price of sugarcane.
predicates.no_state_law_regulates_cane_supply_and_p: No state law authorizes regulation of the supply or purchase of sugarcane in the relevant state.
predicates.state_cannot_unilaterally_fix_price_but_: The state cannot fix the price unilaterally, but the parties may agree to pay more than the central minimum.

issues.definition: If a challenge concerns a state price announcement and no state law regulates cane supply or purchase, the state cannot fix the price unilaterally, though the parties may agree on a higher price.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment quashing a state-fixed sugarcane price must be reconsidered when the deciding court did not examine the state law governing sugarcane supply and purchase.
material_facts: The relevant High Courts quashed state-fixed sugarcane prices while relying substantially on the central price order and an earlier judgment.
Those courts did not examine the applicable state laws regulating sugarcane supply and purchase.
The Supreme Court’s decision established that such state laws may confer power to fix a higher price, depending on their provisions.
issues.conclusion: The judgments were set aside and the matters were remitted to the High Courts for fresh consideration under the applicable state laws.
issues.legal_principle: The existence and scope of state power to fix a higher cane price depend on the applicable state law and must be examined before deciding whether the state price is valid. The Court applied its interpretation of the U.P. Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1953, and directed reconsideration under the relevant laws in the other states, including the Bihar Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1981, the Punjab Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1953, and the Andhra Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1961.

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_quashing_state_cane: An appeal challenges a judgment that quashed a state-fixed sugarcane price.
predicates.applicable_state_regulation_law_not_exam: The court that quashed the price did not examine the applicable state law regulating sugarcane supply and purchase.
predicates.judgment_set_aside_and_matter_remitted_f: The judgment is set aside and the matter is returned for fresh consideration under the applicable law.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a judgment quashing a state cane price without examination of the applicable state regulation law, the judgment is set aside and the matter is remitted for fresh consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Interference is not warranted with an order vacating interim protection where the applicant has not paid the statutory minimum price owed to sugarcane growers.
material_facts: A sugar mill challenged an order vacating interim protection in its price dispute.
The mill had not paid the statutory minimum price to growers, and a substantial amount remained due.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s order and dismissed the special leave petition.
issues.legal_principle: In the circumstances presented, the unpaid statutory minimum price was a sufficient reason not to interfere with the order vacating interim protection.

predicates.special_leave_challenge_to_vacating_inte: A party seeks special leave to challenge an order vacating interim protection in a price dispute.
predicates.statutory_minimum_price_remains_unpaid: The sugar mill has not paid the statutory minimum price owed to growers.
predicates.no_interference_with_order_vacating_inte: The court declines to interfere with the order vacating interim protection.

issues.definition: When a special leave challenge concerns vacated interim protection and the statutory minimum price remains unpaid, the court does not interfere with that order.

issues.legal_issue: Relief cannot be granted in an application when its principal target is not a party to the proceeding.
material_facts: An application in a pending civil appeal principally sought relief against a government that was not a party to that appeal.
issues.conclusion: The application was dismissed because the requested relief could not be granted against a nonparty.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot grant the principal relief sought against a person or government that is not a party to the proceeding.

predicates.application_seeks_relief_against_nonpart: An application principally seeks relief against a person or government that is not a party to the proceeding.
predicates.application_dismissed_for_relief_against: The application is dismissed because the requested relief is directed against a nonparty.

issues.definition: If an application principally seeks relief against a nonparty, it is dismissed on that basis.
